s1.syndrome_frame: Gradual onset of a bony hard, fixed, and lobulated chest mass in a child
salient_findings: Swelling on the right anterior chest
key_facts: 9-year-old boy
Swelling first appeared as a pea-sized nodule three years earlier
Lesion gradually increased to approximately 0.5 cm in diameter
No pain, tenderness, or respiratory symptoms
No other swellings
Mass is bony hard and fixed to the underlying rib
Overlying skin is normal and freely mobile
Tangential chest radiograph shows a bony outgrowth arising from the lateral aspect of the right sixth rib

shortlist.label: Osteochondroma
shortlist.why_kept: Matches clinical description of a bony hard, fixed, and lobulated chest mass

shortlist.label: Chondrosarcoma
shortlist.why_kept: Possible malignant tumor of cartilaginous origin, although less likely given age and lack of symptoms

shortlist.label: Fibrous dysplasia
shortlist.why_kept: Could present as a bony lesion, but typically has a more complex appearance on imaging

shortlist.label: Osteosarcoma
shortlist.why_kept: Malignant bone tumor, but usually presents with more aggressive features and symptoms

shortlist.label: Chordoma
shortlist.why_kept: Rare tumor of notochordal origin, could present as a bony mass, but less likely given location and age

raw.rationale: The lesion's gradual growth, bony hard consistency, and fixation to the underlying rib, along with the radiographic evidence of a bony outgrowth from the rib, are characteristic of osteochondroma.

rejected.label: Chondrosarcoma
rejected.why: Typically presents with pain and more rapid growth, which is not seen in this case

rejected.label: Fibrous dysplasia
rejected.why: Usually involves the medullary cavity and has a ground-glass appearance on radiographs, not a bony outgrowth

rejected.label: Osteosarcoma
rejected.why: Typically aggressive with rapid growth, pain, and systemic symptoms, which are absent in this case

rejected.label: Chordoma
rejected.why: Usually occurs in the axial skeleton, particularly the spine and base of the skull, and has a distinct radiographic appearance
